newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian farmers back genetic engineering.
newsitem.headline: Australian farmers back genetic engineering.

text.p: Australian farmers would need access to genetic engineering to increase the efficiency of food production, New South Wales Farmers' Association president Ian Donges told the association's annual conference.

Farmers also wanted to avoid the need to segregate traditionally produced and genetically modified foods and wished to avoid a need to separately label genetically modified foods, he told the meeting in Tamworth, in northern New South Wales.
Donges described genetically modified food as a huge issue around the world and as currently the biggest source of tension in agricultural matters between the U.S. and the European Union.
"Although we need to be mindful of our customers' concerns, we must also endeavour to progress the debate to ensure access to the latest technology," he said.
Speaking about current crop conditions, Donges said 1997/98 could put the "icing on the cake" for the state's grain industry followubg good to excellent grains years between 1995 and 1997.

He reiterated the farm lobby stand that valid pastoral leases must extinguish native title following a High Court decision last year which increased the land area which may be claimed under native title to 78 percent from 36 percent.
Further court decisions, for example in the Yorta Yorta claim along the Murray River, were expected to determine how far native title spreads throughout Australia, Donges said.
Donges said Australian net farm income, officially forecast at A$2.2 billion in 1997/98, was unsustainably low, despite the recent record grain harvest.
"Marketing arrangements for wool, meat and grains are currently under review and will need to be managed to ensure that structures and policies are in place to maximise returns to farmers," he said.
"On the wider income side, we must continue with the task of tearing down barriers against world trade in agricultural produce," he added.
